newsitem.title: HAITI: Haiti rejects overtures from former dictator.
newsitem.headline: Haiti rejects overtures from former dictator.

text.p: The Haitian government on Monday rejected overtures by former dictator Jean-Claude Duvalier to play a role in the country's future, saying he had no political prospects and would face criminal charges if he returned from exile in France.
"Duvalier can come back if he wants to take the chance of facing the Haitian people," Haitian Foreign Minister Fritz Longchamps told Reuters.

President Rene Preval, in remarks published on Monday in the daily Le Nouvelliste, said that if Duvalier returned to Haiti he would face charges of stealing hundreds of millions of dollars in state funds before he was ousted by a popular uprising more than 10 years ago.
The government response followed a radio address by Duvalier last Tuesday which was taken by his supporters as an indication he might try to return to run in 2000 presidential elections.
The broadcast was the first time the former dicator's voice had been heard in Haiti since he left for France in 1986.
Duvalier, also known as "Baby Doc," asked for pardon and expressed the wish to play a role for change in the country.
A Haitian government attorney said on Monday the government would not actively seek Duvalier's extradition, though.
The government reaction was "a way of calling Duvalier's bluff," government attorney Ira Kurzban said in a telephone interview from his offices in Miami.
He said he doubted Duvalier's address was a serious attempt to return to Haitian politics, saying it was likely aimed at undercutting the democratically elected government.
"The real issue is not Duvalier coming back," he said. "He could not win an election. He couldn't do anything."
Both Longchamps and Justice Minister Max Antoine said exile is not a recognised means of punishment under Haitian law and that Duvalier's exile in France was self-imposed.

Duvalier relied on terror during his 15-year rule to control the population -- following in the style of his father, Francois "Papa Doc" Duvalier, a former country doctor who maintained supreme power over Haiti with sinister police agents and crude superstition.
